ops.new_text: The cardiac-related impedance change in lung EIT frames is several times smaller than the ventilation change (Leathard et al., 1994) <!--ref:Leathard1994PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:quote:ventilatory%20and%20cardiac%20related%20changes%20in%20EIT%20images--> and highly position dependent (Graf and Riedel, 2017) <!--ref:Graf2017PLOSONE--><!--anchor:quote:highly%20position%20dependent-->. Three of our studies precede it: a U-Net for lung segmentation in EIT (Ko and Cheng, 2021a) <!--ref:Ko2021PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:quote:U-Net-based%20approach%20for%20automatic%20lung%20segmentation-->, the semi-Siamese U-Net that separates lung and heart images with one encoder and two parallel decoders (Ko and Cheng, 2021b) <!--ref:Ko2021PLOSONE--><!--anchor:quote:Semi-Siamese%20U-Net%20for%20separation%20of%20lung%20and%20heart%20bioimpedance%20images-->, and heart-related image reconstruction from GREIT frames with optimised loss weights (Ko et al., 2025) <!--ref:Ko2025CurrMedImaging--><!--anchor:quote:Reconstruction%20of%20Heart-related%20Imaging%20from%20Lung%20Electrical%20Impedance%20Tomography-->. Elsewhere, a Siamese network supplied the feature-matching constraint of an unsupervised cardiac-signal separation from chest EIT image series (Zhang et al., 2022a) <!--ref:Zhang2022PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:quote:Deep%20feature-domain%20matching%20for%20cardiac-related%20component%20separation-->. Throughout, *segmentation* names the task of producing a Dice-scored mask, and *separation*, *weak component* and *dominant component* name the mechanism. The semi-Siamese study's discussion states that "the separation effect of the EIT image obtained by the different reconstruction algorithms will be investigated" (Ko and Cheng, 2021b) <!--ref:Ko2021PLOSONE--><!--anchor:quote:the%20separation%20effect%20of%20the%20EIT%20image%20obtained%20by%20the%20different%20reconstruction%20algorithms%20will%20be%20investigated-->, naming the Sheffield back-projection algorithm, a finite-element linearised Newton–Raphson algorithm and GREIT; this paper answers it, with one-step Gauss–Newton as its linearised Newton–Raphson member. A companion simulation study from our group, in review, evaluates the same two arms under GREIT across noise levels; this paper relies on none of its reported findings, re-uses its GREIT-trained networks re-scored here (Section 2.2), and the two are declared related submissions [MATERIAL GAP: preprint DOI, see Related manuscript].

Multi-source training and its failures are documented clinically: pneumonia detection generalised variably across hospitals (Zech et al., 2018) <!--ref:Zech2018PLoSMed--><!--anchor:quote:Variable%20generalization%20performance%20of%20a%20deep%20learning%20model-->, cross-institutional tumour segmentation lost Dice (AlBadawy et al., 2018) <!--ref:AlBadawy2018MedPhys--><!--anchor:quote:Impact%20of%20cross-institutional%20training%20and%20testing--> and multi-site segmentation used site-specific normalisation (Liu et al., 2020) <!--ref:Liu2020TMI--><!--anchor:quote:Multi-Site%20Network%20for%20Improving%20Prostate%20Segmentation%20With%20Heterogeneous%20MRI%20Data-->. The closest analogue to a change of EIT reconstructor is a change of computed tomography (CT) reconstruction kernel: a training-by-evaluation matrix with a pooled row (Hoang-Thi et al., 2021) <!--ref:HoangThi2021DIII--><!--anchor:quote:Which%20reconstruction%20kernel%20should%20be%20used%3F--> and a cross-evaluation varying kernel, slice thickness and dose one at a time (Zeng et al., 2022) <!--ref:Zeng2022MedPhys--><!--anchor:quote:Generalizability%20over%20dose%2C%20reconstruction%20kernel%2C%20and%20slice%20thickness-->.

The three reconstructors are those the original study named (Section 1.2; Gauss–Newton stands for its linearised Newton–Raphson), each at one fixed setting listed in S2 Table. GREIT, the Graz consensus reconstruction algorithm for EIT (Adler et al., 2009) <!--ref:Adler2009GREIT--><!--anchor:quote:GREIT%3A%20a%20unified%20approach%20to%202D%20linear%20EIT%20reconstruction%20of%20lung%20images-->, was built as registered on a 64 × 64 grid (nominal noise figure 0.5, realised 0.602 on a common reference frame). The noise figure (Adler and Guardo, 1996) <!--ref:Adler1996TMI--><!--anchor:quote:regularized%20imaging%20and%20contrast%20detection--> is the ratio of relative noise in the image to relative noise in the measurements, so matching it compares two regularised linear reconstructors at equal noise amplification on the same data. One-step Gauss–Newton (GN) with a Laplace prior was parametrised on GREIT's 64 × 64 grid, its hyperparameter set by bisection to match GREIT's realised noise figure (hp 0.0016, noise figure 0.607). Back-projection (BP) used the Sheffield back-projection matrix (Barber and Brown, 1984) <!--ref:Barber1984JPhysE--><!--anchor:quote:Applied%20potential%20tomography--> distributed with EIDORS (Adler and Lionheart, 2006) <!--ref:Adler2006EIDORS--><!--anchor:quote:an%20extensible%20software%20base%20for%20EIT-->, with no free parameter (noise figure 0.831); its 32 × 32 raster was upsampled two-fold by pixel replication and masked to GREIT's field of view. Because reconstruction settings strongly influence a reconstructor's output (Thürk et al., 2019) <!--ref:Thurk2019PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:quote:Influence%20of%20reconstruction%20settings-->, every result holds for these three operators at these settings.

Two arms share one U-Net encoder (Ronneberger et al., 2015) <!--ref:Ronneberger2015UNet--><!--anchor:quote:U-Net%3A%20Convolutional%20Networks%20for%20Biomedical%20Image%20Segmentation-->, bottleneck, block structure, loss, optimiser schedule and dataset. The encoder takes a 1 × 64 × 64 input through four levels of 32, 64, 128 and 256 channels (two 3 × 3 convolutions with batch normalisation and rectified linear units per level, 2 × 2 max-pooling) to a 512-channel bottleneck; a decoder mirrors it with 2 × 2 transposed convolutions and skip concatenation, 32 channels wide at the finest level, and ends in a 1 × 1 output convolution. Arm D splits at the bottleneck into two decoders of the original width, one per target: the architecture under test. Arm B_wide has one decoder with two output heads, widened by 1.5312 (channel counts rounded to multiples of eight: 48, 96, 192 and 392, fine to coarse) so that its parameter count (10,743,738) matches D's (10,811,298) within one percent. The primary contrast, D minus B_wide, holds supervision, data, schedule and capacity constant, leaving only whether the decoder is split. Fixed-budget comparison of branch structures follows the branched multi-task literature (Vandenhende et al., 2020) <!--ref:Vandenhende2020Branched--><!--anchor:quote:Deciding%20what%20layers%20to%20share-->, and an adequately configured baseline at comparable compute is the control whose absence lets a new architecture appear to beat a U-Net (Isensee et al., 2024) <!--ref:Isensee2024nnUNetRevisited--><!--anchor:quote:A%20Call%20for%20Rigorous%20Validation%20in%203D%20Medical%20Image%20Segmentation-->. Matched parameter count is not matched architecture, and other controls (matched floating-point operations, an unsplit decoder of the original width) were not run.

Sharing one encoder between two decoders is hard parameter sharing (Caruana, 1997) <!--ref:Caruana1997MTL--><!--anchor:quote:Multitask%20Learning-->. The two L1 losses were summed with fixed weights of 1.0 each, a scope decision: the original study proposed the branch with a multi-weighted loss and credited their interaction, and this study evaluates the branch alone. Fixed weights are defensible, since unit or tuned fixed weights have matched specialised multi-task optimisers in controlled comparisons (Kurin et al., 2022; Xin et al., 2022) <!--ref:Kurin2022Unitary--><!--anchor:quote:In%20Defense%20of%20the%20Unitary%20Scalarization%20for%20Deep%20Multi-Task%20Learning--> <!--ref:Xin2022MTOHelp--><!--anchor:quote:Do%20Current%20Multi-Task%20Optimization%20Methods%20in%20Deep%20Learning%20Even%20Help%3F-->; learned weighting (Kendall et al., 2018) <!--ref:Kendall2018--><!--anchor:quote:Multi-task%20Learning%20Using%20Uncertainty%20to%20Weigh%20Losses--> was not tested. Training settings, fixed before registration: Adam at 1 × 10⁻³ with cosine decay to 1 × 10⁻⁵, batch 16, at most 200 epochs, early stopping on validation loss (patience 20, best weights restored), L1 loss on the float target, no output activation, no augmentation, and one dataset-wide normalisation affine, a fixed location–scale standardisation estimated on that dataset's training split and applied to inputs and targets, called below that dataset's affine. Thirty seeds (0 to 29) per arm and training row were trained on one machine (Mac mini M4, MPS backend; a seed fixes data order and initialisation, but the backend does not guarantee bit-identical re-execution, so a seed is a replicate, not an exactly reproducible run); seed-to-seed variability can be large (Renard et al., 2020) <!--ref:Renard2020SciRep--><!--anchor:quote:Variability%20and%20reproducibility%20in%20deep%20learning%20for%20medical%20image%20segmentation-->, and here it is of the order of the effects at stake. The GREIT row reuses seeds 0 to 29 of the companion study's 20 dB training (same machine and code; PyTorch 2.8.0), trained between 2026-09-24 16:26 and 2026-09-26 00:44 and scored on 2026-09-26, before the registered state was hashed (17:41); the registered text declares this reuse and names that row as the reference for the two R1 cells (Section 2.5); a between-campaign difference is confounded with every contrast pairing a GREIT-trained network with one trained here (Section 3.4).

The primary endpoint is heart-channel Dice on the quarter-amplitude set, the region above one quarter of the image's peak; the registered 25% lies inside the 20–35% band recommended for region-of-interest definition on functional EIT images, a band defined on per-pixel statistics rather than on a reconstructed amplitude (Pulletz et al., 2006) <!--ref:Pulletz2006ROI--><!--anchor:quote:20-35%25%20of%20the%20maximum%20standard%20deviation%20or%20regression%20coefficient-->. The endpoint is computed in image units on the test split and averaged over seeds; one Dice point is 0.01. The reference for each reconstructor is that reconstructor's own single-organ heart reconstruction, not the anatomical heart. This is registered and follows from the task: for a network separating the cardiac component of a reconstructed image, the correct answer is by definition what that reconstructor produces when only the heart is present. Scoring against an anatomical mask would fold each reconstructor's blur and bias into the endpoint; comparing reconstructors by image quality is outside this paper's claims, and Dice against an anatomical reference was not computed. The lung channel is reported in every cell, not tested, with the registered expectation of no arm difference.

Fig 2 shows the design. Three single-reconstructor rows give the matched cells; six off-diagonal cells evaluate a trained row on another operator without retraining; two pooled rows train on all three reconstructors (8,640/1,080/1,080 frames), one with a single affine over the pooled split (mixed, registered) and one with each source standardised by its own training-split affine before pooling (mixed-ps, first addendum); three leave-one-reconstructor-out rows train on two sources with per-source affines (5,760/720/720 frames) and are evaluated on the third, never seen in training (loro, second addendum). The training-by-evaluation crossing follows an EIT cross-condition design (Jeschke et al., 2025) <!--ref:Jeschke2025Sensors--><!--anchor:quote:Robustness%20to%20Electrode%20Displacement-->. The per-source affine is fixed, not learned, because this study measures the network's response to a source difference and a learned normaliser would absorb part of it (Section 4.3).

Table 4 gives the four SHA-256 states of the preregistration file, what each governs, and what had been read when each was written; S3 Table quotes every decision rule and fixed interpretation sentence verbatim. The registered state (2026-09-26) fixed R1, R3 and M1 with their rules, interpretations in both outcomes, n = 30 and the pilot before any arm of this study was trained; the companion study's GREIT networks, whose reuse the registered text declares, already existed (Section 2.2). Two deviations were recorded on 2026-10-03 before any cell was read: the pilot's acceptance band for GN's noise figure predated the change of matching rule from GREIT's nominal to its realised value (the rule changed before hashing; the band did not), and BP's single-organ peaks were offset from GREIT's by up to 2 pixels against a registered tolerance of one pixel (2 pixels is one pixel of BP's native grid). No hypothesis, endpoint, arm, setting, sample size or rule changed; BP was analysed as registered, with the offset noted beside every BP cell. Two further decisions, taken after cells had been read, are recorded in Table 4 and S2 Table with timing and consequence: the registered secondary scoring path is listed but not read, because it moves the output's background off zero (Section 3.2), and the registered interpretation of a falsified M1 is quoted but not applied to the two cells whose input was unreadable (Section 3.3). Neither changes a verdict.

The minimal dataset (per-seed Dice for every cell, the aggregated results file, gate and seed-0 diagnostic files) and the four preregistration states with their hash file are deposited on Zenodo [MATERIAL GAP: Zenodo DOI, minted at submission; the deposit is prepared]; the data-generation, training, scoring and figure code is in the project repository under a tagged release [MATERIAL GAP: repository tag, set at submission]. Checkpoints are available from the corresponding author; artificial-intelligence use is disclosed in the Acknowledgments.

Table 2 and Fig 2 give the six registered off-diagonal cells, scored with the training set's affine. The difference of differences, Δ(X→Y) − Δ(X→X), was negative in five cells (−1.07 to −10.05 points) and positive with an interval containing zero in the sixth (BP→GN, +2.97, CI −0.12 to +5.84), so all six R3 cells are falsified. The fixed reading for a falsified cell is, verbatim, "the tolerance seen in the noise sweep is specific to that kind of shift" (S3 Table); the noise sweep it names is the companion study's, whose result this paper does not use. The shift tested here is a change of reconstructor; other kinds, such as noise level, were not tested.

Three qualifications belong to the result. Pooling is expected to help and is not claimed as a finding, as the preregistration stated. It is not free: the mixed-ps row reached a similar best epoch to the single-source rows (median 57 and 74.5 epochs against 56 to 72.5) on three times as many frames per epoch, so each run took about three times the optimisation steps and wall time, which this design cannot separate from the benefit of three renderings per geometry. And the normalisation is source-aware. For the GREIT cell of M2′ and for every contrast that pairs a GREIT-trained network with one trained in this study, the GREIT networks come from the companion study's campaign (Section 2.2), so a between-campaign difference is confounded with the contrast; those networks also score the R3 cells GREIT → GN and GREIT → BP (Table 2). M3′, the share of the registered-path no-retraining loss that pooling removed, is in Table 2 in points (+34.7/+44.8 for GN→BP and +15.1/+11.7 for BP→GN in the two in-range cells; the four cells crossing GREIT carry the degenerate or over-range note).

Table 3 and Fig 2 give the held-out rows. L1 compares the control arm on the held-out reconstructor with the same arm on the in-pool mixed-ps row, against a margin of ±1.0 point fixed before training. The differences were −61.8 points (CI −65.1 to −58.5) on GREIT, −15.8 (−16.7 to −14.9) on GN and −35.8 (−39.4 to −32.7) on BP (D beside, untested; Table 3). No interval approaches the margin; L1 is falsified in all three cells. The fixed reading applies to each reconstructor in turn, verbatim: "the recipe stays in-pool only for that reconstructor, and the loss is reported as the cost of deploying on an unseen reconstructor" (S3 Table). The addendum expected three falsifications with losses of 5 to 30 points: met on 3 of 3 verdicts and 1 of 3 magnitudes (GN). The six in-pool comparison cells of the same rows scored 0.957 to 0.967, the level of the diagonals, so the two-source pools were not deficient: the networks failed only on the unseen source. The loss order, GN smallest and GREIT largest, would follow if the loss reflects how well the pool covers the held-out reconstructor; that mechanism was not tested, and the order does not rank reconstructors. Because the reference image moves with the reconstructor (Section 2.3), each loss is an upper bound on the input-side generalisation loss.

A leave-one-source-out comparison is usually reported as a non-significant difference, as in a four-centre segmentation study that read median Dice of 0.76 pooled against 0.74 held out, p = 0.18, as compatibility (Holzschuh et al., 2024) <!--ref:Holzschuh2024RadiatOncol--><!--anchor:quote:multicentric%20datasets-->. Non-significance cannot establish equivalence; a margin can (Lakens, 2017) <!--ref:Lakens2017SPPS--><!--anchor:quote:Equivalence%20Tests-->. This study fixed one before the runs and the test was falsified: the deployment recipe of pooled training with a per-source affine is in-pool only, a tested restriction. The conclusion is insensitive to the margin, since every interval lies 14 to 58 points outside it and would lie outside ±5 or ±10 points as well, a post-hoc sensitivity statement, not a change of margin. Within this study's scope the term "reconstructor-agnostic", the authors' own first-addendum wording, is falsified, and any source-aware statement must read "for the three conventional reconstructors in the training pool, with the deployed reconstructor's own affine". Within the search of Section 1.3, one precedent exists for equivalence testing on segmentation Dice (Venkatesh et al., 2026) <!--ref:Venkatesh2026MedPhys--><!--anchor:quote:Performance%20benchmarking%20of%20deep%20learning%20models-->; it is no convention of the field.

The registered pooled row failed for a reason neither the preregistration nor the pilot anticipated, found only when the network's normalised inputs were plotted after scoring. Reconstructed EIT amplitude is not a shared currency: within one algorithm it changes with the reconstructed quantity (Grychtol and Adler, 2014b) <!--ref:Grychtol2014PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:quote:Choice%20of%20reconstructed%20tissue%20properties-->, and across algorithms it differed here by two orders of magnitude. Where source differences are modest, as among multi-centre magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners, whose unitless intensities we take to differ by far less than two orders of magnitude, the choice among normalisation methods changes Dice by less than 0.02 (Albert et al., 2023) <!--ref:Albert2023ApplSci--><!--anchor:quote:Comparison%20of%20Image%20Normalization%20Methods%20for%20Multi-Site%20Deep%20Learning-->; the failure here was not a wrong choice among such methods but the absence of any per-source step. That step can also live in batch-normalisation layers (Karani et al., 2018) <!--ref:Karani2018MICCAI--><!--anchor:quote:Across%20Scanners%20and%20Protocols--> or be learned across datasets (Delisle et al., 2021) <!--ref:Delisle2021MedIA--><!--anchor:quote:Realistic%20image%20normalization%20for%20multi-Domain%20segmentation-->; this study kept it at the input and fixed, so the network's response to the source difference could be measured alone.

The claim that training-source diversity improves out-of-distribution performance (Mårtensson et al., 2020) <!--ref:Martensson2020MedIA--><!--anchor:quote:clinical%20out-of-distribution%20MRI%20data%3A%20A%20multicohort%20study--> was neither seen nor contradicted: in the two in-range cells, two-source pooling against single-source no-retraining showed no evidence in either direction, with only two sources, thirty seeds, intervals of ±2 to ±7 points, and a different affine policy on the two sides, which alone moved these cells by 4 to 14 points in E1. In-pool and out-of-pool performance are reported separately because pooled models can look strong internally and weak externally (Zech et al., 2018) <!--ref:Zech2018PLoSMed--><!--anchor:quote:Variable%20generalization%20performance-->. A reconstructor change is one kind of acquisition shift (Castro et al., 2020) <!--ref:Castro2020NatCommun--><!--anchor:quote:Causality%20matters-->, and that tolerance depends on the kind of shift has a CT analogue in kernel changes being costly where slice-thickness changes were not (Zeng et al., 2022) <!--ref:Zeng2022MedPhys--><!--anchor:quote:reconstruction%20kernel%2C%20and%20slice%20thickness--> and a general one in corruption benchmarks, where tolerance differs by corruption type (Kamann and Rother, 2021; Boone et al., 2023) <!--ref:Kamann2021IJCV--><!--anchor:quote:Robustness%20of%20Semantic%20Segmentation%20Models%20with%20Respect%20to%20Common%20Corruptions--> <!--ref:Boone2023NeuroImage--><!--anchor:quote:out-of-distribution%20and%20corrupted%20data%20in%20MRI-->. Two next steps lie outside this study: learned harmonisation, which outperformed the location-scale baseline this fixed affine amounts to for CT radiomics (Du et al., 2022) <!--ref:Du2022EurRadiol--><!--anchor:quote:harmonization%20of%20CT%20reconstruction%20kernels-->, and training-distribution randomisation (Billot et al., 2023) <!--ref:Billot2023MedIA--><!--anchor:quote:any%20contrast%20and%20resolution%20without%20retraining-->, which three fixed reconstructors are not.

Of twenty verdict cells, twenty were falsified; twelve posed the question they were designed for, and eight (four R3 and two M1 cells with unreadable input, and the two held-out L2 cells whose floors were 9.5 points) were falsified in cells the design failed to pose or could hardly have confirmed (Sections 3.2, 3.3 and 3.6). Registered Reports return positive results far less often than the standard literature, 44% against 96% in one comparison (Scheel et al., 2021) <!--ref:Scheel2021AMPPS--><!--anchor:quote:Comparing%20the%20Standard%20Psychology%20Literature%20With%20Registered%20Reports-->, and a null against a matched baseline is a kind of result exposed to under-reporting in computational fields (McGreivy and Hakim, 2024; Borji, 2018; Varoquaux and Cheplygina, 2022) <!--ref:McGreivy2024NatMachIntell--><!--anchor:quote:Weak%20baselines%20and%20reporting%20biases--> <!--ref:Borji2018ImaVisComput--><!--anchor:quote:Negative%20results%20in%20computer%20vision--> <!--ref:Varoquaux2022NPJDigitMed--><!--anchor:quote:methodological%20failures%20and%20recommendations-->. Preregistration exists to make such results reportable (Nosek et al., 2018; Chambers and Tzavella, 2021) <!--ref:Nosek2018Prereg--><!--anchor:quote:The%20preregistration%20revolution--> <!--ref:Chambers2021NatHumBehav--><!--anchor:quote:Registered%20Reports-->, and simulation comparisons can be made to favour any method unless their rules are fixed in advance (Pawel et al., 2024) <!--ref:Pawel2023BiomJ--><!--anchor:quote:Questionable%20research%20practices%20in%20comparative%20simulation%20studies-->.

The obvious objection is that the registered part governed the least informative cells and every number a reader will quote came from the addenda; three facts answer it. The addenda were hashed before their runs, with rules, margins and expectations written down, and the hit rates are reported as they fell (M1′ 3 of 3 verdicts, 1 of 3 magnitudes; L1 3 of 3, 1 of 3; L2 3 of 3, 0 of 3); no registered verdict was revised. Both addenda were written to test outcomes unfavourable to the authors' own recipe, and found them: the first left the branch below the floor, and the second denied the pooled recipe any generalisation beyond the pool at the pre-fixed margin. The expectations written before those runs anticipated the falsifications, so the results met rather than surprised the authors' stated expectations, and in two of the three L1 cells the loss exceeded the expected range. And the second addendum's rows were those a simulated review round (Acknowledgments), recorded in the repository before the addendum was written, had asked for.
